John Moses and Joseph Kirkland (eds.), History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (Chicago and New York: Munsell & Co., 1895). Read here for the town before 1836: the immigration chapter 'From Village to City - 1830 to 1837 - the Balloon Age' at printed pages 78-79 and 87-101, the early taverns and hotels at pages 560-561, the 'Real Estate and Insurance' chapter at pages 541-542, the packing trade at page 389, the fire department at pages 207-208, the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy quoted from Blanchard at page 35, and the Biographical sketches of P. F. W. Peck, Philo Carpenter, John Dean Caton and Alexander N. Fullerton at pages 570-577 and 584; and, for the shore of 1812 (T-0471), the chapter 'The Massacre' at pages 49-50, 54 and 60-61 - the low, discontinuous sand-hills south of Twelfth Street, the scattered cottonwoods on the bank's lower reaches, and the two 'Massacre trees' of Eighteenth Street with Mrs. Kinzie's word that they were saplings in 1812.

transcribes.note: PRINTED AT LENGTH AND NOT MERELY CITED. At pages 34-35 the volume introduces the Kinzie and Clybourn genealogy as 'best told by Rufus Blanchard ... He says:' and sets the whole passage as a block quotation, which is why bk_mose1_019 - Benjamin Hall's 1830 arrival and the town's first tannery - is a reading of Blanchard through Moses and Kirkland and not of Moses and Kirkland. This project does not hold Blanchard and cannot check the transcription. Blanchard in turn credits Benjamin Hall himself for the detail, so the chain to the fact is three deep and the claim says so.
transcribes.work: Rufus Blanchard, Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (Wheaton, Ill.: R. Blanchard & Co., 1881)

what_it_does_not_supply: MOST OF WHAT IT WAS FETCHED FOR. Of the forty-nine lead surnames the Newberry index flagged against this work, thirteen earned a claim, twenty-one appear only outside the pre-1836 window, eight appear early and say nothing usable, one (`black`) is only ever the adjective, four are unresolved because the volume carries a surname one character from the index card's spelling, and two are absent outright. The full row-by-row result is committed at data/research/books/moses_kirkland_v1_lead_surnames.json so the next run does not pay for the search twice.

VOLUME 2, WHICH IS HALF THE WORK. Only volume 1 is read. The Newberry cards do not say which volume they cite, so an absence recorded here may simply be in the other book, and every ABSENT verdict in the lookup file says so on itself.

AN INDEPENDENT VOICE. It is a compilation of 1895 and it names its own authorities on the pages read: Andreas for Garrett's $1,800,000 of auction sales, Bross's History of Chicago page 38 for the earliest deeds, the Story of Chicago page 130 for Caton's election tally, Hurlbut's Chicago Antiquities pages 37-8 for the pre-1830 settler list, S. R. Beggs's West and Northwest page 95 for the Black Hawk alarm, and Rufus Blanchard's Discovery of the Northwest and History of Chicago (1881) quoted at length for the Kinzie-Clybourn genealogy. Where the sentence itself credits another work, the claim says so and the citation must go to that work and not to this one.
A SINGLE ADDRESS IN THE MODERN SENSE, and no street numbers. Positions here are corners, lots, blocks, a river bank and a tree.

ANY DATE FINER THAN THE YEAR for two things this project wanted finer: Caton's marriage, which is given as '1835' with the scene date sitting in the middle of it, and the Hubbard-Marsh packing partnership, which is 'later'.

CONSISTENCY WITH ITSELF. Page 89 dates Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings to 1832 while page 570 has Peck's occupied in the fall of 1831; page 207 forms the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company on 7 October 1835 while page 570 has it organised on 20 October 1835. Both readings of each are recorded and neither is adopted.
what_it_supplies: A TRADE CENSUS OF THE WHOLE TOWN, at page 95: the State census taken between 1 September and December 1835 counted 3,297 people, forty-four stores, two book stores, four druggists, two silversmiths and jewellers, two tin and copper manufactories, two printing offices, two breweries, one steam saw-mill, one iron foundry, four storage and forwarding houses, eight taverns, one lottery office, one bank, five churches, seven schools, twenty-two lawyers, fourteen physicians, and a lyceum and reading room. The project had no denominator for its business layer and this is one - for December 1835 and not for July.

A BUILDING WITH FOUR OF THE FIVE FIELDS data/structures/ WANTS, at page 90: John S. C. Hogan's story-and-a-half log storehouse, 45 by 18 feet, at the angle where Lake and South Water streets meet, with the post office partitioned off inside it from 2 November 1832.

TWO RESIDENCES STATED AS SUCH, which is the field the town is thinnest in: Rev. Jeremiah Porter lodging and keeping his study in the second storey of Peck's store from May 1833 (page 571), and John Dean Caton renting the back room and attic of Dr Temple's Temple Building from December 1833, sleeping in the attic and practising law in the back room, and sub-letting desk-room in it to his competitor Spring (page 577).

BUSINESSES GIVEN BY CORNER, LOT OR LANDMARK: Dole's and Peck's first frame business buildings at the south-east corners of South Water and Dearborn and of South Water and La Salle (page 89); Peck's two-storey frame store of black walnut brought from Detroit, occupied in the fall of 1831 (page 570); Sylvester Marsh killing beef under an old elm on the open prairie at what became Monroe Street from the winter of 1833-4 (page 389); William Jones's lots 2 and 7 in block 17 fronting Water and Lake (page 542).

OCCUPATIONS AND ARRIVALS for men this project already holds: Philo Carpenter as the town's first druggist, arriving within a month before 19 August 1832; Benjamin Hall as proprietor of the first tannery ever established there, arriving 1830; Dole, Clybourn, the Noble brothers and Gurdon S. Hubbard beginning the slaughtering and packing trade in 1832; the 1833 spring arrivals including Caton, Kimball and Asahel Pierce; and Hubbard's permanent residence dated to 1832 by the compiler's own reason for leaving him off a list.

TWO PRESENCE LISTS: the twenty-two men who signed the Pioneer Hook and Ladder Company roll on 7 October 1835 (pages 207-208), and, unread and left for its own ticket, the 'LIST OF ACTUAL SETTLERS AT CHICAGO, PRIOR TO 1830' at pages 78-79, about thirty rows with nativity, year and remarks columns.
ONE STATEMENT ABOUT THE GROUND OF THE SCENE, at page 79: the winter of 1834-5 was open, with little snow, front doors standing open all winter, and cattle living on grass on the river bank.

endings.text: You go to the call in a plain made coat, and keep the travelling coat for tomorrow's work. By the second tune nobody can tell a Holbrook coat from a New York tailor's, and by the third nobody cares.
You go to the call brushed and neat in the coat you came in, with a length of good broadcloth in mind for later. In a town of slippers and brogans, you fit right in.

evidence.locator: Chicago Democrat, 10 June 1835, p. 3, col. 2 (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c010, copy line 'Chicago, June 10, 1835'); Chicago American, 13 June 1835, p. 3, col. 6 (claim chicago_american_1835_06_13#c012). Transcription-mediated readings.
evidence.text: John Holbrook advertised clothing, boots and shoes, wholesale and retail, 'on South-Water st. one door from Dearborn street', signed himself agent for the manufacturers, and said he would be receiving additions to his assortment every fifteen or twenty days through the season; the American's printing adds hats.

evidence.reasoning: An agent for the manufacturers who keeps 'a large assortment of the named articles' and restocks by shipment is selling finished goods made elsewhere. The card names no cutting, measuring, fitting or making to order, so the stop claims none; that the goods were ready-made is read from the card's words, not stated in them.
evidence.text: Holbrook's stock was made clothing sold from stock, not a tailoring service.

evidence.reasoning: Both printings give 'one door from Dearborn' on South Water Street. The structure record reads the door count as the next front east of the Chicago American's corner office under the owner's corner-ordinal ruling, because that makes three addresses printed on this face consistent; its size and form are borrowed from neighbours on the face and graded reconstructed.
evidence.text: The store stood on the south side of South Water Street, one door east of Dearborn; the side of Dearborn is a reading and the building is reconstructed.

evidence.locator: Chicago Democrat, 5 Nov 1834, p. 3, col. 2 ('Fall and Winter Goods', claim chicago_democrat_1834_11_05#c007). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: Harmon, Loomis & Co.'s fall and winter notice lists fancy and staple dry goods, among them broad cloths, cassimeres, domestic cloths, satinets, Peter Sham, goats' hair camlet, woollen and cotton flannels, Russia duck and canvas.

evidence.reasoning: The Chicago American of 20 June 1835, p. 1, col. 2 ('At Wholesale and Retail', claim c006) opens its list with dry goods but its transcription is damaged there and names no cloths. That the firm stocked broadcloth and the rest on 1 July 1835 is carried from the 1834 notice by the June one; no source records a cloth, sale or price on the scene date.
evidence.text: In June 1835 Harmon, Loomis & Co. still advertised staple and fancy dry goods at wholesale and retail from their store in South Water Street; the cloth list itself is carried forward from the November 1834 notice.

evidence.reasoning: The north side of South Water was the river frontage and Andreas gives the south-west corner to the Chicago Democrat's office, so the record takes the south-east. The advertisements name South Water Street only.
evidence.text: Andreas puts the Harmon and Loomis store at the corner of Clark and South Water and never says which corner; the marker's south-east corner is the structure record's choice.

evidence.locator: Vol. 1, printed p. 132, boarding-house paragraph; p. 303, Jeremiah Porter biography.
evidence.text: Andreas names Mrs Rufus Brown as a boarding-house keeper in his account of 1833, and places Brown's log house behind Peck's store.

evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives the position only relative to Peck's store. The structure record sets the house directly south of the store's footprint on the same lot line and grades the coordinate reconstructed, so the stop calls the spot reconstructed.
evidence.text: The boarding house is placed directly behind Peck's store at the south-west corner of South Water and LaSalle; its distance behind the store is not documented.

evidence.reasoning: The stop uses the structure record's scene-date phase and its continuity argument. A building label is an identity, not proof of a continuing tenancy; the visitor's lodging there is part of the invented errand.
evidence.text: The boarding house is an exterior stop in the July 1835 scene; Andreas's account of 1833 does not prove that the visitor, or anyone, lodged there that day.

evidence.locator: Ch. XVII, 'Chicago in 1831' — the Wolf Point houses, Mark Beaubien's house just completed.
evidence.text: Wau-Bun describes the Sauganash in 1831 as 'a pretentious white two-story building, with bright-blue wooden shutters'.

evidence.locator: 10 June 1835 (Vol. II No. 8), p. 2, col. 5, the paragraph on the town's public houses (claim chicago_democrat_1835_06_10#c001). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: The Chicago Democrat of 10 June 1835 reported that the Sauganash had been repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste.

opening.text:
JAUNT: A DECENT COAT. You have a call to pay at the Sauganash this evening and work to begin tomorrow, and your only coat is still grey with road dust. In this town that may not matter much. At a Chicago ball in 1834 the New York writer Charles Hoffman found 'a complete medley of all ranks, ages, professions, trades and occupations', and watched 'a pair of Cinderella-like slippers' dance opposite 'a brace of thick-soled brogans'.

Still, you would like to look decent. South Water Street sells clothes ready made and cloth by the yard. See what the stores advertise, stop at your boarding house to think it over, and decide what you will wear tonight.

premise: Look at what two South Water stores advertised to wear, and choose how to go to a call at the Sauganash.

stops.narrative: A coat you could wear tonight.
stops.text: Start one door from Dearborn at John Holbrook's. On 10 June 1835 he advertised clothing, boots and shoes, wholesale and retail, as agent for the manufacturers, with new goods arriving 'every fifteen or twenty days'. That is the new way to dress in a boom town: coats made in the eastern shops and shipped in by lake, ready to wear tonight. No tailor, no fitting, no waiting.

stops.narrative: A better coat, one day, but not by tonight.
stops.text: A block west at Clark, Harmon, Loomis and Company sell dry goods. Their winter card listed broadcloths, cassimeres, satinets, flannels and goats' hair camlet, with heavy Russia duck and canvas, and in June they still advertise dry goods, wholesale and retail. Fine cloth makes a fine coat, but cloth is not a coat: somebody still has to cut and sew it, and that takes longer than one afternoon.

One more block west, to Mrs Rufus Brown's log boarding house behind Peck's store. The store in front was the village's first two-storey frame, built of lumber 'sawed from black walnut trees' and 'brought from Detroit by a boat'; the town has dressed up a good deal since. Lay the choice out on the bed you share: a call tonight wants neatness, tomorrow's work wants wear, and one coat has to serve both.

choices.consequence: A plain made coat of the kind Holbrook's card offers, ready tonight.
choices.label: Wear a ready-made coat

choices.consequence: Go neat in what you have; cloth for a work coat can be made up later.
choices.label: Brush the old coat

stops.narrative: The call is tonight, whatever you wear.
stops.text: On to Lake and Market and the Sauganash, white with bright-blue shutters in Juliette Kinzie's memory, and repaired and newly fitted up this June. Its landlord, Mark Beaubien, is 'the fiddler par excellence of the town', and when he plays, Judge Caton said, he could 'set every heel and toe in the room in active motion'. Nobody will look at your coat for long. Decide what you wear.
